segments.title: Designing a Royal Navy within a whole-defence budget
segments.summary: The fleet exercise is uncosted, yet it confines itself to coherent capabilities based on existing or projected equipment and keeps the rest of defence in view.
segments.body: The exercise asks what Royal Navy force structure would be coherent if national leaders chose to fund it. It does not supply a cost estimate, but it rules out fictional technology, extreme fleet sizes, and equipment without an existing or projected basis. The scope stays mainly naval because the Army and Royal Air Force deserve assessments from people who know those services in equal depth. These limits turn a fantasy-fleet prompt into a disciplined comparison of capabilities, support requirements, and public choices.

evidence.note: Introduces the uncosted but equipment-bounded force-design exercise and explains its mainly naval scope.

segments.title: Interservice rivalry and the CVA-01 lesson
segments.summary: The CVA-01 dispute illustrates how attacking another service's programme can make the case for cutting both, weakening national defence and each service's own position.
segments.body: The CVA-01 dispute supplies the warning. The Royal Navy lost its carriers, the Royal Air Force did not receive the planned strike aircraft, and the RAF soon lost much of its V-force and long-range bomber capability. Arguments that dismiss another service's carriers, tanks, artillery, or aircraft give ministers a ready case for moving finite public money elsewhere. Education, health, and policing are legitimate demands on the same taxpayers, so defence advocates strengthen their case by explaining what their own capability contributes. Service preservation should remain subordinate to the defence of the United Kingdom.

evidence.note: Uses the CVA-01 dispute to argue for positive capability cases instead of interservice attacks over finite public funding.

segments.title: A five-ship core for global reach
segments.summary: The proposed fleet is built around two strike carriers and three large amphibious ships, with logistics and escorts treated as the means that make distant power useful.
segments.body: An American-football analogy explains the relationship between headline ships and support: a quarterback needs an offensive line long enough to act. The five-ship core consists of two Queen Elizabeth-class strike carriers and three large amphibious ships. Escorts and the Royal Fleet Auxiliary provide the fuel, stores, protection, and troop movement that let those ships operate far from Britain. Global reach comes from the whole force, with each category built around what the carriers and amphibious ships must do.

evidence.note: Sets out the proposed force categories and the supporting role of logistics and escorts.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth-class air groups as mixed aviation forces
segments.summary: A carrier air group combines F-35B fighters, anti-submarine Merlins, commando-lift helicopters, and airborne early-warning aircraft, so fighter numbers tell only part of its capacity.
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth class has room for a substantial mixed air group. One illustrative load combines two F-35B squadrons with Merlin helicopters for anti-submarine warfare, commando lift, and airborne early warning. That mixture connects fleet air defence and strike with submarine detection, troop movement, and surveillance beyond the horizon. Carrier capacity depends on the missions the air group can sustain, including the compromises between fast jets and helicopters.

evidence.note: Describes the proposed Queen Elizabeth-class troop capacity and mixed F-35B and Merlin air group.

segments.title: Canberra-class ships as amphibious and aviation insurance
segments.summary: Three Canberra-class-sized landing helicopter docks would combine dock, stores, accommodation, hangar, and flight deck capacity while providing limited back-up for a carrier or amphibious ship in refit.
segments.body: An LHD combines a dock, flexible vehicle and stores deck, accommodation, hangar, and flight deck in one hull. Paired with a Bay-class successor, a Canberra-sized ship could carry roughly a third to half of a modern brigade, including artillery and manoeuvre elements. Three LHDs would give the force reciprocal cover: one could operate a limited F-35B strike group when a carrier was unavailable, while a Queen Elizabeth-class carrier could assume part of the aviation and troop role if extra dock landing ships covered the missing dock capacity. The LHD is suited to many lesser threats, while a peer opponent with modern missiles calls for the greater capability of a strike carrier.

evidence.note: Explains Canberra-class LHD capacity, task-force scale, and limited substitution with the carriers.

segments.title: Forward-based amphibious shipping and fleet sustainment
segments.summary: Forward-based landing and logistics ships would handle routine regional tasks, leaving carrier and amphibious task groups available as a larger reaction force.
segments.body: Smaller landing and logistics ships would remain in the Indian Ocean, South Atlantic, and Pacific, allowing the carrier and LHD groups to act as reaction forces. A forward-based ship could handle a limited emergency, support an ally, or establish a regional foothold before a larger formation arrived. Eight Tide-class tankers and four solid-support ships would sustain the fleet across long Pacific distances. The numbers include spare capacity for wartime losses, since a peacetime efficiency calculation could leave too little resilience once ships are damaged or sunk.

evidence.note: Covers forward-based landing ships, tanker numbers, and additional solid-support ships.

segments.title: Three escort groups for carrier and amphibious task forces
segments.summary: Six Type 45 destroyers and nine Type 26 frigates would form three high-end escort groups sized around the simultaneous protection of carrier and amphibious forces.
segments.body: The escort calculation starts with the ships required to protect the carrier and LHD groups. Each of three high-end formations would pair two Type 45 air-defence destroyers with three Type 26 anti-submarine frigates. Britain could operate a carrier group and an amphibious group simultaneously, leaving the third formation to cover availability or reinforce an allied operation. Canadian, Australian, American, and other allied escorts could enlarge the screen. Common task-group organization would make that support easier to integrate.

evidence.note: Sets out the proposed Type 45 and Type 26 numbers, three-group structure, and allied reinforcement model.

segments.title: Personnel growth as the cost of a larger fleet
segments.summary: The larger escort and task-group structure would require roughly 25 percent more Royal Navy personnel, making recruiting and crewing part of the capability proposal rather than an invisible assumption.
segments.body: A larger fleet also requires more sailors. The rough estimate is a 25 percent increase in Royal Navy personnel, which would make recruiting, training, and retention a major programme in their own right. Hull totals alone conceal this human operating requirement. Crewing capacity belongs in the force plan from the start.

evidence.note: Estimates the personnel increase required by the proposed fleet and connects it to recruiting and operational options.

segments.title: Type 45 successors and Type 31 wartime roles
segments.summary: Nine Type 45 successors would preserve high-end escort availability and allow occasional forward presence, while Type 31 frigates would reinforce battle groups as close escorts in war.
segments.body: Nine successors to the Type 45s would guarantee the three basic escort groups and leave options for another formation or a semi-permanent high-end regional presence. The heavily used Daring-class destroyers may have too little service life left for a useful reserve fleet after replacement. Type 31 frigates sit outside the core high-end screen during routine operations. In war, they would join carrier and amphibious groups as close escorts.

evidence.note: Explains Type 45 successor numbers, regional presence, reserve prospects, and Type 31 wartime close-escort duties.

segments.title: Type 31s for persistent regional presence
segments.summary: A larger Type 31 force would keep ships in the Falklands, Gibraltar, Bahrain, and Singapore, giving Britain a visible regional stake before a crisis demands a task group.
segments.body: Forward-based Type 31s would provide routine presence through observation, training, partner reassurance, and an initial response. Pairs at the Falklands, Gibraltar, Bahrain, and Singapore would cover the South Atlantic and Antarctic approaches, Mediterranean trade routes, the Gulf and Indian Ocean, and Southeast Asia. Ships back in Britain would refit, prepare relief crews, and provide a home-water escort when another power sent a major warship near the coast. Britain needs ships in a region if it expects current knowledge and a credible voice in decisions there.

evidence.note: Explains forward basing and presence missions for ten to twelve Type 31 frigates.

segments.title: A modular River-class patrol force
segments.summary: A modified Batch 3 River class could combine heavier guns, Martlet missiles, StanFlex modules, UAV support, a stern ramp, and optional towed sensors for flexible regional patrol work.
segments.body: The Batch 3 concept adapts an existing River-class hull with modular equipment for different regional missions. Its proposed fit includes a twin 40-millimetre Bofors mounting, two 30-millimetre guns with Martlet missiles, three StanFlex positions, a UAV hangar, and a stern ramp. The ramp could launch boats, uncrewed systems, or a towed sonar. These patrol ships could escort mine-countermeasures forces, counter piracy, protect merchant shipping, exercise with partners, and visit ports too small for a Type 31.

evidence.note: Describes the modified River-class equipment fit and its flexible patrol roles.

segments.title: Naval stations as diplomatic and humanitarian networks
segments.summary: Regional naval stations led by senior captains would coordinate ships, diplomats, partner relationships, disaster relief, and the advance knowledge that makes a fleet more useful in a crisis.
segments.body: Regional stations would organize the ships around Bahrain, Singapore, the Falklands, Gibraltar, and home waters. A senior captain holding a commodore's pennant could coordinate each area without creating a permanent one-star post. Joint staffs and the Foreign Office would use port visits, exercises, shipboard meetings, and naval hospitality to build access. Disaster-relief modules, cranes, boats, landing ships, and Royal Marines would support humanitarian work. Long-standing local relationships could then provide warning and practical help before a larger crisis.

evidence.note: Outlines regional stations, command appointments, diplomacy, and disaster-relief roles.

segments.title: Amphibious vehicles for Royal Marines and strike brigades
segments.summary: Using amphibious combat vehicles across Royal Marine and strike formations would let troops drive ashore, reinforce one another, and reduce dependence on landing craft for every movement.
segments.body: The preferred common vehicle is the US Marine Corps Amphibious Combat Vehicle, used by an amphibious brigade and two strike-amphibious brigades. Royal Marines could secure an entry point, then Army formations arriving aboard Point-class ships could reinforce them with compatible equipment. Heavy assets would still use landing craft, but personnel carriers could drive ashore directly and move across inland waterways. They could also cross through the Channel Tunnel and continue across France, or return under their own power in the "reverse Dunkirk" scenario described here, subject to refuelling. The Sir Galahad example shows the danger of keeping troops concentrated aboard a transport while they wait to disembark.

evidence.note: Makes the case for common amphibious vehicles across Royal Marine and strike formations.

segments.title: Continuous at-sea deterrence as a standing posture
segments.summary: A ballistic-missile submarine kept continuously at sea avoids the visible activation and deployment that can make a nuclear force more escalatory during a crisis.
segments.body: Continuous at-sea deterrence treats the nuclear force as a standing posture. Britain lacks an acceptable land area for the weapons in this proposal, and aircraft or space basing introduces risks the plan rejects. A submarine already on patrol does not need a visible readiness change as tensions rise. Fueling, arming, or deploying a nuclear force during a crisis would send a new signal that an opponent might read as an immediate threat.

evidence.note: Contrasts a continuously deployed submarine deterrent with the escalatory signal of activating a nuclear force during a crisis.

segments.title: Convertible submarine tubes and a five-hull deterrent reserve
segments.summary: Five compatible Dreadnought-type hulls could support three declared ballistic-missile boats, two conventional cruise-missile SSGNs, and reserve capacity against accidents or refit delays.
segments.body: Four boats are normally associated with guaranteeing continuous at-sea deterrence. This proposal builds five compatible Dreadnought-type hulls while publicly assigning only three to the ballistic-missile role. Inserts in the other two boats' large missile tubes would let them carry conventionally armed cruise missiles as SSGNs, providing a day-one strike option when conflict was expected in advance. If collision, refit delay, or another accident removed an SSBN from service, one SSGN could return to the deterrent role. The common class combines a declared reduction in ballistic-missile boats with physical redundancy.

evidence.note: Discusses five compatible hulls, three declared SSBNs, two cruise-missile SSGNs, and reserve capacity after an accident.

segments.title: Britain's nuclear-submarine shipyard limits fleet numbers
segments.summary: Britain's single nuclear-submarine construction yard constrains how quickly SSBNs, Astute-class boats, and a future attack-submarine class can be built, even when a larger fleet is desirable.
segments.body: A larger nuclear attack-submarine force still depends on industrial capacity. Britain has one yard producing these boats, which must finish seven Astute-class submarines while building five Dreadnought-type hulls. A successor attack-submarine class of seven to nine boats would then follow through the same production system. Orders become operational boats only through sustained shipyard throughput and a skilled workforce.

evidence.note: Explains how the single nuclear-submarine construction yard constrains SSBN, Astute, and successor production.

segments.title: Conventional-submarine partnership and Falklands basing
segments.summary: A conventional submarine successor could use a Japanese design or a joint sensor-led project, with two boats based in the Falklands for South Atlantic awareness.
segments.body: A Japanese partnership offers two routes to a conventional successor: buy an established Soryu-derived design or join the proposed 3,000-ton Japanese programme. British Astute-style sensors could form part of the joint design. Canada might join such a procurement effort, and Australia might also reconsider if its contemporary French programme continued to struggle. Two boats based in the Falklands would add South Atlantic awareness and deterrence, leaving four available from Britain.

evidence.note: Covers Japanese conventional-submarine options and the rationale for Falklands forward basing.

segments.title: National presence within allied collective strength
segments.summary: Alliances multiply British power, but dependence on American logistics and post-Cold War European cuts mean Britain still needs its own regional forces if it wants influence and warning.
segments.body: Falklands basing aims to establish strength and regional relationships before the South Atlantic or Antarctica becomes a sharper area of competition with China. Collective Western power depends heavily on American logistics, bases, forces, and money. European governments had legitimate reasons to reduce defence spending after the Cold War, but this interpretation holds that many cut global presence too deeply. In a globally connected society, alliances still leave Britain needing its own ships and submarines for local knowledge, diplomatic weight, and a voice in crisis management.

evidence.note: Connects South Atlantic basing to Chinese competition, American alliance support, European defence cuts, and the need for national presence.

segments.title: Royal Marine battle groups and strategic lift
segments.summary: Four regular and two reserve Royal Marine battle groups could form larger amphibious formations, but their scale depends on Point-class strategic lift as well as LHD and dock-landing-ship availability.
segments.body: Four regular and two reserve Royal Marine commandos would operate as self-contained battle groups, with any three able to form a brigade. Under normal availability, two LHDs and two Bay-class successors would carry only part of that maximum formation. Point-class ships would provide the remaining strategic lift. Six future lift ships with better accommodation would make it practical to deploy the additional troops and equipment without forcing them into inadequate living conditions.

evidence.note: Summarizes the Royal Marine battle-group structure and dependence on Point-class lift.

segments.title: A joint P-8 force for maritime patrol
segments.summary: Sixteen regular and eight reserve P-8 Poseidons would provide maritime patrol reach from Diego Garcia, the Falklands, and the United Kingdom.
segments.body: The plan calls for sixteen regular P-8 Poseidons and eight reserve aircraft, raising the total to 24. Basing or detachments at Diego Garcia, the Falklands, and in Britain would extend maritime patrol coverage and provide surge capacity. Similarities between P-8 aircrew work and civilian Boeing operations support the proposed reservist contribution. Joint Royal Navy and Royal Air Force crewing would spread the manpower burden and give both services a reason to defend this maritime capability in government.

evidence.note: Sets out a larger P-8 fleet, regional basing, reserves, and a joint-service operating model.

segments.title: Archer-class training craft and reserve links
segments.summary: Expanding the Archer-class force to twelve craft would preserve practical training links between universities, reservists, and the wider Royal Navy.
segments.body: The plan retains the River-class patrol ships and adds twelve Archer-class training craft. University Royal Naval Units and reservists use the small vessels for practical experience at sea. This gives students and part-time personnel a direct connection to naval operations as well as shore establishments. Training craft support the recruiting and reserve base needed by a larger combat fleet.

evidence.note: Proposes twelve Archer-class craft and connects them to university and reserve naval training.

segments.title: Mine countermeasures and survey ships for port access
segments.summary: Forward-based mine countermeasures vessels and a retained hydrographic squadron would keep overseas approaches, British ports, and operational waters usable.
segments.body: Four mine-countermeasures vessels would remain in the Gulf, with further units based around Singapore and British home waters. Portsmouth, Plymouth, Southampton, and the Medway are examples of ports where mines could obstruct naval and commercial movement. Forward forces depend on accessible operating bases and home ports. The hydrographic squadron, including HMS Scott and the smaller Echo-class ships, supplies the charting and seabed knowledge required for safe operations.

evidence.note: Covers forward-based and home-water mine countermeasures plus the retained HMS Scott and Echo-class survey force.

segments.title: A global Royal Marine regiment for smaller missions
segments.summary: Small Royal Marine companies embarked on forward-deployed landing ships would give the fleet a rotating force for independent regional missions while preserving larger commandos for battle groups.
segments.body: The proposed global regiment consists of company-sized Royal Marine units separate from the commandos that form amphibious battle groups. Each forward-deployed landing or support ship would normally carry a company commanded by a major for independent regional missions. Eight companies would keep four deployed while the others rotated through relief, training, and recovery at home. Four regular and two reserve commandos would remain available for the larger battle groups and brigade structure.

evidence.note: Explains the proposed global regiment, company deployments, rotation, and commando structure.
